newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Resurgent inflation checks Zimbabwe's stocks.
newsitem.headline: Resurgent inflation checks Zimbabwe's stocks.

text.p: Rising inflation is threatening Zimbabwe's share market again after a gap of over four years, but analysts and brokers say the market, 1996's second best emerging markets performer, should weather the storm aided by strong growth in the economy and corporate profits.
The broader industrial index, on the ascendancy since the year began, has crumbled more than 6.6 percent or 723.85 points since touching an historic high of 10,980.10 on April 24.

Short-term interest rates have risen from around 16 percent last month to range between 22 and 23 percent on fears that a recent bout of price increases will rekindle annual inflation. In 1992 inflation, together with severe drought, hacked the industrial index back by close to 70 percent.
Analysts and brokers believe interest rates rises have drawn money and buyers from the market as the central bank, the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe, sought to contain inflation.

"The market will have to adjust to higher interest rates," Savvas Kyriakides of market analysts Dataworld said. "But I do not believe that returns on the money market are now that attractive to institutional investors."

In the year to April inflation rose to a 10-month high of 22.4 percent from 19.9 percent in March, prompting some analysts to revise this year's forecast average above last year's 21.7 percent and raising the spectre of a return to higher interest rates.

"Certainly there is a lot of nervousness from an institutional investor's point of view as to where rates are going and that will obviously impact on the market," said one broker, who declined to identified.
The 59-share industrial index, the Zimbabwe Stock Exchange's main barometer, grew 15.75 percent in the first quarter while the secondary mining index rose 8.62 percent.

Quincor James Capel managing director Julian Vezey sees softness and volatility in the index in the second quarter as small investors, attracted by the firming interest rates ditch the market but he envisages no repeat of the 1992 debacle.
"The market will generally be soft but I do not see it crashing," said Vezey, whose firm holds most of the funds of the exchange's approximately 30 foreign funds active on the market.
Kyriakides, who believes the market's bull run is still strong, says results expected in the next few weeks when about 30 percent of the market will report, will lift industrials.
Zimbabwe's economy, which last year posted its strongest growth in more than a decade, is expected to further expand by more than five percent this year.

"The bull run is still there and I think the results which are coming, including Meikles and Delta, will see a resurgence of the market," Kyriakides said, forecasting the index will remain locked between 10,000 and 11,000 until August.
